text:
The Eagles are adding some insurance under center.

Philadelphia has signed quarterback Joe Milton off the Cowboys’ practice squad, according to multiple reports.

Milton appeared in four games for Dallas in 2025, throwing for 183 yards on 24 attempts with one touchdown and two interceptions.

The Cowboys traded for Milton before last season after he had an eye-opening season finale for the Patriots in 2024 — completing 22-of-29 passes for 241 yards and a touchdown in a 23-16 win over the Bills.

He again flashed his potential — and tantalizing arm-talent — during this preseason with a three-touchdown game against the Cardinals.

However, the 26-year-old Milton was waived by the Cowboys on Sept. 1 and placed on their practice squad two days later with Sam Howell being named the backup.

Milton will likely join Tanner McKee and rookie Cole Payton on the Eagles’ active roster as the emergency quarterback, meaning he’s unlikely to see much playing time barring any more injuries.

The move comes after news broke Thursday that Hurts would be out indefinitely with a superficial blood clot in his calf, just the latest in a myriad of losses that have hit the Eagles in recent weeks.

The team’s statement revealed that Hurts’ blood clot was discovered via ultrasound before their game in London against the Jaguars last Sunday. A second ultrasound Wednesday revealed the movement of the blood clot, putting Hurts on the shelf indefinitely as the Eagles “determine the appropriate course of treatment.”

McKee will likely be the Eagles’ starter for the time being as they try to get back on track after a 2-3 start in a wide open NFC East.

Sunday’s game against the Panthers will mark McKee’s third career start. His previous two career starts were in end-of-season matchups after the Eagles had secured their spot in the postseason.

The Eagles face Milton’s former Cowboys team in their first of two meeting in a Week 7 “Monday Night Football” matchup on October 26th.

Milton was drafted in the sixth round of the 2024 NFL Draft with the 193rd overall pick by New England.

Milton spent the first three years of his college career at Michigan before transferring to Tennessee.

text:
Even after losing in Week 5, the Atlanta Falcons are clearly trending in the right direction under head coach Kevin Stefanski. The team has gone 2-1 since Michael Penix Jr.'s return, barely losing to the Baltimore Ravens in overtime last weekend.

The Falcons have another tough test coming up against the Chicago Bears in Week 6. Not only is head coach Ben Johnson's team an offensive juggernaut, but the Bears are expecting to get star QB Caleb Williams back this week.

In today's Falcons Wire Recap, Bijan Robinson and Drake London take over as the NFL's best RB-WR duo, Kyle Pitts lands on fantasy sit 'em list, PFF projects Atlanta to take a left tackle in a new mock draft, and we look at the latest injury updates ahead of Sunday's game vs. the Bears.

Falcons release safety Jammie Robinson

The Falcons released defensive back Jammie Robinson on Thursday evening. Robinson, who spent much of the last two seasons on the Falcons' practice squad, was signed to the active roster before Sunday's loss to the Baltimore Ravens. The 25-year-old entered the league as a fifth-round pick with the Carolina Panthers back in 2023.

After playing in 21 games over his first two seasons with the Panthers, Robinson signed with the Falcons in 2025 and appeared in six games. Over his four-year NFL career, Robinson has recorded 23 tackles (16 solo) while contributing primarily on special teams.

Since the Falcons still have a practice squad spot available, we wouldn't be surprised to see Robinson back in Atlanta before Sunday's game against the Bears.

Falcons-Bears injury report: Michael Penix, Caleb Williams updates

Michael Penix Jr. was a full participant at Thursday's practice for the second day in a row. The third-year quarterback is expected to play against Chicago. As for Bears quarterback Caleb Williams, he also appears on track to play on Sunday. The former No. 1 pick was a full participant on Chicago's latest injury report. Falcons defensive end Cameron Thomas was added to Thursday's report (see below).

QB Michael Penix (ribs): FP

LT Jake Matthews (groin): FP

LB Divine Deablo (hamstring): FP

DE Za'Darius Smith (neck): LP

DE Cameron Thomas (groin): LP

CB C.J. Henderson (groin): DNP

RT Jawaan Taylor (rest): DNP

Drake London says Falcons offense nowhere near its ceiling

Michael Penix Jr. re-established his lethal connection with top wide receiver Drake London, who's totaled over 400 receiving yards over the last three games. To hear London tell it, this offense still has a lot of room to grow. Here's what he said about it earlier this week, per Josh Kendall at The Athletic.

“The fun part about this (offense) is that we are nowhere near our ceiling. I truthfully believe that,” London said. “I think we’re going to be … hard to deal with, especially when we clean up some of these little things.”

Falcons have NFL's top RB-WR duo going into Week 6

After scoring just 16 total points in their first two games of the season (8.0 points per game), the Falcons have put up 103 points over the last three weeks (34.3 points per contest) with Penix in the lineup.

Bijan Robinson currently leads the NFL with 580 rushing yards, surpassing Kansas Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker for the top spot going into Week 6. Drake London's production has been off the charts with Penix slinging the rock. The former USC standout's 488 receiving yards rank fourth in the NFL.

Between Robinson and London, the duo has accounted for 1,220 total yards - the highest total of any running back-wide receiver duo in the NFL this season.

Michael Penix Jr. 'good to go' vs. Bears in Week 6

Falcons QB Michael Penix Jr. exited Sunday's loss to the Ravens in the fourth quarter with a rib injury and did not return. The third-year quarterback's lengthy injury history has been regurgitated ad nauseam, however, it doesn't sound like Penix is going to miss any time with his rib injury.

"We’re good and I feel good to go this week, so that’s the plan," Penix said following Wednesday's practice. "MRI/scans were all positive... It’s not always comfortable but I made every throw out there today."

Falcons take OT in PFF's new 2027 NFL mock draft

Trevor Goosby from Texas has been the most popular mock pick for Atlanta so far for Round 1, but today we have a new name to digest. A new 2027 NFL mock draft from Pro Football Focus has the Falcons rolling the dice on Jordan Seaton from LSU at No. 14 overall.

"Seaton would give the Falcons a succession plan for Jake Matthews at left tackle, with the veteran currently in his 13th season. LSU's left tackle has earned a 79.1 PFF pass-blocking grade so far in 2026 and produced a 93.5% PFF pass-block win rate on plays where he has been left to block without help." - Gordon McGuinness, PFF

Grady Jarrett excited to face former team

Former Falcons defensive tackle Grady Jarrett, who's undoubtedly one of the best players in franchise history, signed with the Bears in 2025. Jarrett will return to Mercedes-Benz Stadium for the first time since departing in free agency.

The former fifth-round pick out of Clemson spent 10 seasons in Atlanta and served as the face of the defense for the bulk of that span. Jarrett, a Georgia native, recorded 496 tackles (267 solo), 126 QB hits and 36.5 sacks over 152 games with the Falcons.

Hurts had a blood clot in his leg.
That would be relevant information, especially as to anyone thinking about wagering hard-earned money through one of the sportsbooks that sponsor the NFL (and in which any NFL team owner can hold up to five-percent of the total equity).
The official injury report from the Eagles didn’t begin to paint the picture as to Hurts’s true condition and status.
text:
The outside world (including anyone considering placing wagers on the game and/or the specific player’s performance) had no idea that Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts had developed a blood clot in his leg before the team’s Week 5 game in London against the Jaguars. The Eagles, and the league, knew otherwise.

The statement issued by the Eagles on Thursday made it clear that the team was aware of the situation, and that the clot was revealed by an ultrasound examination performed after the team arrived in London. “Throughout our time in London and this week, we have remained in communication with the league office regarding the matter,” the Eagles said.

Given that the Eagles specifically said the team had “remained in communication with the league office,” we asked the league office whether it had anything to add — specifically as to the question of why Hurts’s status for the game wasn’t changed at any time to “questionable.”

“The team was in contact with the league throughout the process, including the morning of the game,” an NFL spokesperson said via email on Friday morning. “A team would need to make a public announcement immediately if there was any question as to his availability or if he would be impacted in any way. That was not the case here. We would not want a team to list a player as ‘questionable’ on gameday morning when the team knows with 100 percent certainty that he will play in the game. . . . Hurts played 100 percent of the snaps on offense during the game and there was no issue.”

That’s fine, but wasn’t there, at some point, a question as to Hurts’s availability? From the moment it was decided to seek an ultrasound to the moment that the doctors reviewed and analyzed the results, there was an obvious question as to the specific condition that had prompted Hurts to land on the injury report on Friday with a “calf” injury, and whether that condition could keep him from playing.

While Hurts played and took every snap, the league’s current policy (with which the Eagles complied) creates a donut hole of inside information that isn’t shared with the public. Hurts had a blood clot in his leg. That would be relevant information, especially as to anyone thinking about wagering hard-earned money through one of the sportsbooks that sponsor the NFL (and in which any NFL team owner can hold up to five-percent of the total equity).

Whether the NFL revamps its injury-reporting rules on its own or whether the mandate comes from Congress or a regulatory agency, it seems inevitable that more will be required, one of these days. The official injury report from the Eagles didn’t begin to paint the picture as to Hurts’s true condition and status.

Given that, between Saturday and Tuesday, the blood clot moved (making Hurts unavailable for Week 6), it would have been appropriate for the public to know that there was a possibility that, between Saturday and the start of Sunday’s game, the blood clot could move or Hurts’s condition could otherwise deteriorate.

And, yes, it’s possible to have genuine concern for the player’s health while also pointing out the flaws in the current rules that work to the disadvantage of the betting public. Every injury necessarily represents a negative impact on the player’s health. The question becomes whether or not there is sufficient transparency.

Hall has not played since Week 3 due to a quad injury.

Braelon Allen, who ran for 116 yards and a touchdown last week against the Browns, will get be RB1.

After being limited in practice on Wednesday, Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez was a full participant in Thursday's practice, according to the team's injury report.

That upgrade points to a potential return this week, as New England takes on the Jets on Sunday. Gonzalez has missed the last two games while dealing with a shoulder injury.

Chiefs wide receiver Rashee Rice did not practice on Thursday with multiple injuries, making it likely that Kansas City will be without their top receiver on Sunday. Rice, who left the Chief's Week 4 win over the Raiders early after pulling up awkwardly, is listed as dealing with issues with his hamstring and his knee.

The Chiefs will return to the field on Sunday after a bye last week, but multiple receivers being wiped out with injuries has raised questions. (Things appear worrying enough that Kansas City appears to be weighing other options, like signing Tyreek Hill.)

For the time being, Tanner McKee is tasked with steadying the Eagles' ship. And the waters around Philadelphia are getting pretty rocky these days.

Jalen Hurts being diagnosed with a superficial blood clot is the latest in a deepening injury problem, ruling the quarterback out for Sunday's game against the Panthers. The timing couldn't be worse with the Eagles having lost three straight, the past two in heartbreaking fashion.

McKee was named Hurts' replacement. Andy Dalton had been Hurts' backup to open the season but was cut after an interception against the Bears in Week 3.

McKee has started two career games, both coming in meaningless Week 18 games. Last season, after the Eagles had clinched a playoff spot the week before, McKee completed 21-of-40 passes for 241 yards, one TD and one interception in the 24-17 loss to the Commanders.

The Eagles listed 24 players on this week's injury report, not to mention the five offensive players on injured reserve. The offensive line also took recent hits with the sudden retirement of right tackle Lane Johnson and the trade of left guard Cam Jurgens.

Hurts' injury could be week to week, so it appears McKee could be the starting quarterback during a key stretch of the Eagles' season. After the Panthers, the Eagles face each of their NFC East rivals leading into the Week 10 bye — Monday night against the Cowboys, at the Commanders and home against the division-leading Giants.

Read more here.

The Houston Texans have ruled out running back David Montgomery, safety Jalen Pitre and receiver Tank Dell for Week 6's matchup in London versus the Jacksonville Jaguars. Neither player will make the trip overseas.

Neither Montgomery (groin) nor Pitre (shoulder) have participated in practice this week, after sustaining injuries during Week 5's 26-3 win over the Tennessee Titans.

Dell (knee) was a full participant on Wednesday and Thursday. He missed the entire 2025 season and the first 5 games of 2026 while recovering from a serious injury in which he tore multiple ligaments and damaged his meniscus in 2024.

The status of Arizona Cardinals running back Jeremiyah Love is up in the air, particularly after the rookie has now missed practice for the second straight day with an ankle injury.

Love, the No. 3 overall pick in this year's draft, has gotten off to a slow start this season.

text:
Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts will miss Sunday's game against the Panthers because of a superficial blood clot in his calf, the team announced Thursday.

In a statement, the Eagles said that Hurts visited the training room after a practice on Oct. 8 for treatment on his calf, informing the staff that he had been cleated during the game against the Rams on Oct. 4. He practiced in full that week.

The staff performed an ultrasound on Hurts when he arrived in London on Saturday "out of an abundance of caution," and it revealed a superficial blood clot that he could play through.

"Our medical staff and doctors in London reviewed the results and concluded that activity and mobility were important and that Jalen could safely play," the statement said. "Doctors recommended a follow-up ultrasound within 72 hours of the game and the return flight to Philadelphia."

According to the Cleveland Clinic, "superficial thrombophlebitis, or superficial vein thrombosis, is a blood clot that occurs in veins under the skin (superficial veins)."

On Sunday, Hurts completed 21 of 40 passes for 220 yards and a touchdown in the 19-17 loss to the Jaguars. He rushed for two yards, his lowest output of the season.

MORE BY JIMMY HASCUP

"Jalen played without limitation in the game Sunday, received treatment on Monday and Tuesday, and practiced in full on Wednesday, as reflected in the practice report," the Eagles said. "On Wednesday night, a follow-up ultrasound revealed movement in the small blood clot. Jalen will be out for Sunday's game vs. the Panthers as we determine the appropriate course of treatment. His health and safety are our highest priority."

Wrote Dr. Brian Sutterer on X, "Oo boy - if this has progressed to a deep vein clot instead of lower risk superficial (Hurts) could be looking at the end of his season. Treatment for that would be blood thinners often for multiple months and the standard is no contact sports while on blood thinners."

Wrote Dr. Tom Christ on X: "Report that he has a superficial blood clot in his lower leg, not a deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Still, this is medically complicated and needs cautious care. DVTs are far worse and would have him out for months, SuVT can still cost substantial time if he needs to go on anticoagulants. Right now with the limited intel released there's no way to project the rest of his season and time missed. We'll await more reports."

text:
SANTA CLARA — Christian Kirk was a spectator for the first five games of the regular season.

Now, he is getting closer to making a difference for the 49ers.

Kirk has been sidelined for nearly three months with a calf injury. The 49ers opened his practice window on Thursday, and now it is up to him to earn his spot off injured reserve and onto the 53-man roster.

“I believe I have a lot of really good football left,” Kirk said on Thursday. “In no way, shape or form, I thought about anything other than that. It's just all about working to get my body back to feeling great, to be able to go out and play.”

Kirk, 29, is a nine-year NFL veteran. He has 432 receptions for 5,415 yards and 30 touchdowns in his career. Last year, he caught 28 passes for 239 yards and a touchdown in 13 games with the Houston Texans.

He was ultra-productive in the postseason, catching 10 passes for 164 yards and two touchdowns in two playoff games for Houston.

There is an opportunity for Kirk to make an impact with the 49ers. Deebo Samuel is expected to be out until after the bye week with a hamstring injury. Demarcus Robinson is nearing a return from a high-ankle sprain. Rookie De’Zhaun Stribling could be out until late-November after undergoing ankle surgery.

San Francisco 49ers

Find the latest San Francisco 49ers news, highlights, analysis and more with NBC Sports Bay Area and California.

In addition, the team’s top wide receiver, Mike Evans, sat out practice with ribs and Achilles soreness. Evans is expected to be available to play Monday night against the Washington Commanders at Levi’s Stadium.

Kirk went through limited practice on Thursday, as he hopes to get up to speed quickly. Other than Evans, the other receivers on the 49ers’ 53-man roster are Brandin Cooks, Jordan Watkins and Jacob Cowing.

The 49ers are one of just three unbeaten teams in the NFL at 5-0 and all alone atop the NFC West standings.

Kirk said he is looking forward to making a contribution toward victories as the season progresses.

“It's like riding a bike,” He said. “I’ve been doing it for a while. And so for me, it's just getting back out there, getting integrated with the guys.

“Obviously, it's been hard not being out there. But it’s been really cool to watch day-in and day-out, how this team comes to work every single day, for it to be able to carry over on Sundays.”

Through his previous eight NFL seasons, Kirk played nine games against the 49ers — mostly during his first four NFL seasons with the Arizona Cardinals.

So he thought he knew a lot about the organization. Still, it has been enlightening seeing how the team operates behind the scenes.

“But now being in the building, and just seeing the approach, seeing the mentality, the mindset day-in and day-out, I think it's been the coolest thing for me to see," Kirk said. "Just the leadership and how those guys take over.

“I’m just ready to be a part of it on the field.”

text:
There is renewed concern about whether enough is being done to prevent the youth sports concussions following a major study that found at least a quarter of NFL players are expected to develop a degenerative brain disease.

“What’s happening when these individuals are younger? How many little hits are they getting that leads to them having CTE? And what can we do at that younger age group to prevent these athletes from getting that?” asked Dr. Nirav Pandya, a pediatric orthopedic surgeon with UCSF Benioff who specializes in sports medicine for young athletes.

Concussions in general affect around two million teenagers and children in the U.S. every year, according to the National Center for Health Statistics.

Boys tackle football has the highest rate of concussions, according to the CDC, and girls soccer is number two. Girls in general have a higher change of sports-related concussions than boys, the agency said, in part because girls may report more and health care professionals like athletic trainers are less likely to be at girls’ practices and games to identify injuries.

California’s student athlete concussion protocol

In California, school coaches are required to take an online training course on concussions. If they suspect a concussion, they must remove the student athlete from the game or practice for at least that day until cleared by a licensed health care provider. If a concussion is confirmed, the student must complete a gradual return-to-play protocol lasting at least seven days.

“I think the tough thing with all of this is that you are basing it on a kid reporting symptoms and someone identifying them,” said Dr. Pandya who said he recently had a patient whose concussions went undiagnosed for over a year.

“He had horrible headaches, had problems learning for over a year and had multiple concussions and hadn't gotten treatment,” Dr. Pandya said. “A concussion, there’s no MRI; no blood test for it.”

Ben Nguyen’s concussion story

The Investigative Unit

Have a tip for The Investigative Unit? Call 1-888-996-TIPS.

Earlier this year, Ben Nguyen, a senior at Archbishop Mitty High School in San Jose, California, says he suffered a serious concussion during a wrestling match.

“I felt incredibly nauseous,” he recalled.

Nguyen shared cell phone video of the moment he got concussed. It showed his opponent go in for a takedown when Nguyen responds by trying to flip the other student over his own body.

“His should and neck were kind of in my chin area,” he said. “The impact kind of went straight to my head.”

The impact wasn’t obvious, but the symptoms afterward were.

“I couldn’t think as fast anymore…I was like throwing up in the bus ride. I was throwing up right after my match as well,” Nguyen said.

Nguyen said he felt a little nervous about telling his coach and athletic trainer, who’s a sports health care professional on the team.

“The impact looked so subtle. I was kind of scared of them being like, ‘Oh, there’s nothing, you can go back,’” Nguyen said. He said that didn’t happen and his school took his injury seriously. However, he admits, it’s easy for students to get around the concussion protocols if they want.

“I have a friend in football who had all the hallmark symptoms of concussions, he just lied on the survey to get back into practice,” he said.

NBC Bay Area reached out to Archbishop Mitty High School. The school declined to participate in this story. The California Interscholastic Federation, which established the state’s student athlete concussion protocol, said it’s important for everyone involved to make sure the return-to-play process is followed.

The solutions, the science, and the debate

“If we can empower kids to understand that it's okay to speak up. Number two, the system, athletic trainers, physical therapists, anyone who's looking over these kids.Then, I think there are more drastic things that we talk about like, how can we decrease the number of chances or times that someone can get hit? Maybe that means delaying when kids start playing tackle football,” Dr. Pandya said.

It’s some of those drastic suggestions that continue to get pushback.

“My big concern is when we hear results about people who play the most elite level, that there's a reaction of looking at, well, what do we do at the youth level? And these are very different games,” said David Camarillo who is Associate Professor of Bioengineering, (by courtesy) Mechanical Engineering and Neurosurgery at Stanford University.

Camarillo has been studying concussions for the past 15 years testing thousands of helmets in his lab, CamLab, in Stanford.

The results he’s talking about come from a recent study published in the British Medical Journal showing at least a quarter of NFL players will likely develop a neurodegenerative disease like CTE. The NFL said it’s aware of the study, and it’s ensuring its community has access to expanding resources. Camarillo believes the science points to urgent action needed at the professional level.

“Does it mean kids shouldn't play sports? I don't think we have enough information to say yes to that,” Camarillo said.

When asked what’s the harm in taking preventative action in case certain youth sports are connected to developing CTE later in life, Camarillo said he believes taking action at an individual level is perfectly fair.

“I think it's a very different thing to make a law, to make public policy that affects everybody, that takes away a right to choose. That ought to have scientific evidence behind it,” he added.

Why isn’t there evidence? The British Medical Journal study relied on hundreds of NFL players donating their brains to science after they die. We don’t have that kind of data on our young athletes today.

The Investigative Unit spoke to numerous doctors, researchers, and students about this issue over the past several weeks. All said the best solution right now is education and schools fostering a culture where students feel encouraged to report concussion symptoms.

“If it wasn't for like my prior knowledge or like my friends or like me witnessing it first-hand, I probably would have lied to get back into wrestling,” Nguyen said.

title: Jets safety Minkah Fitzpatrick says he will appeal fine for hit on Browns receiver KC Concepcion
description:
New York Jets safety Minkah Fitzpatrick told reporters on Thursday that he was fined by the NFL for his helmet-to-helmet hit on Cleveland Browns receiver KC Concepcion during Week 5's 17-12 win.
The play in question occurred during the first quarter when Concepcion went up for a deep throw from Deshaun Watson and was hit hard by Fitzpatrick.
In addition to the collision with Fitzpatrick, the rookie receiver's head hit the MetLife Stadium turf, causing his neck to bend forward.
Fitzpatrick then referred to Browns coach Todd Monken calling the hit "a bang-bang play" and saying he didn't think the safety was a dirty player.
"I understand why I got the penalty," Fitzpatrick added, via the New York Daily News.
text:
New York Jets safety Minkah Fitzpatrick told reporters on Thursday that he was fined by the NFL for his helmet-to-helmet hit on Cleveland Browns receiver KC Concepcion during Week 5's 17-12 win. However, the nine-year veteran intends to appeal the fine.

The play in question occurred during the first quarter when Concepcion went up for a deep throw from Deshaun Watson and was hit hard by Fitzpatrick. Two flags were quickly thrown by officials and the Jets safety was flagged for a 15-yard penalty.

Concepcion was down on the turf for several minutes before trainers helped him to his feet. He was immediately taken to the locker room and soon ruled out for the remainder of the game.

Closer angles on the hit showed that Concepcion may have been knocked out, with his eyes rolling back as he laid on the field. In addition to the collision with Fitzpatrick, the rookie receiver's head hit the MetLife Stadium turf, causing his neck to bend forward.

Fitzpatrick did not say how much he was fined. A first offense for "impermissible use of the helmet/launching" carries a $23,882 fine, while a second offense draws a $47,762 deduction, according to the NFL website.

"It was a football play, in my opinion," Fitzpatrick said. "Obviously, you don't like to see anybody get hurt. I'm happy to see he's back and practicing this week."

Fitzpatrick then referred to Browns coach Todd Monken calling the hit "a bang-bang play" and saying he didn't think the safety was a dirty player.

While Concepcion did return to practice, as Fitzpatrick mentioned, he was a limited participant on Wednesday and Thursday as he continues to be in the NFL's concussion protocol.

"I understand why I got the penalty," Fitzpatrick added, via the New York Daily News. "It wasn't for targeting or hitting him in the head. It was for hitting a defenseless player. In my opinion, when a receiver has the ball, you have every right to hit him as long as you are not hitting him in the head."

Fitzpatrick may have also drawn an additional fine for committing a facemask penalty earlier in the game on Concepcion in which the receiver's helmet was ripped off. If so, he didn't indicate he incurred another fine.

Browns fans already held a grudge against Fitzpatrick for a hit on running back Nick Chubb that caused a serious, season-ending knee injury in 2023. The safety was with the Pittsburgh Steelers at the time.

text:
The Philadelphia Eagles revealed that quarterback Jalen Hurts has been dealing with a calf injury, which involves a blood clot.

Originally, per the team, Hurts informed the Eagles' training staff that he was cleated in the calf during the team's Week 4 game against the Los Angeles Rams, with an ultrasound later showing a superficial blood clot, but the quarterback was cleared to play in their Week 5 game against the Jacksonville Jaguars in London.

"Jalen played without limitation in the game Sunday [Week 5 against the Jaguars], received treatment on Monday and Tuesday, and practiced in full on Wednesday, as reflected in the practice report. Throughout our time in London and this week, we have remained in communication with the league office regarding the matter. On Wednesday night, a follow-up ultrasound revealed movement in the small blood clot," the Eagles said in a statement on Thursday afternoon.

"Jalen will be out for Sunday's game vs. the [Carolina] Panthers as we determine the appropriate course of treatment. His health and safety are our highest priority."

With Hurts out, Philadelphia's quarterback room includes the third-year Tanner McKee, who has made two NFL starts, and rookie Cole Payton.

Through five games, Hurts, a three-time Pro Bowler, has totaled 933 passing yards, eight passing touchdowns, three interceptions and an 84.7 passer rating, while completing 57.8% of his passes.

Hurts' passer rating and completion percentage are each career lows since becoming the Eagles' full-time quarterback in 2021. He has also rushed for 107 yards and one touchdown.

After winning their first two games of the season against the Washington Commanders and Tennessee Titans, the Eagles have lost three consecutive games to the Chicago Bears, Rams and Jaguars. text:
HENDERSON, Nev. -- Las Vegas Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty, who has been battling ankle and foot injuries, said he's feeling "great" ahead of Sunday's home game against the Buffalo Bills.

"I'm ready to go," Jeanty said.

Added coach Klint Kubiak: "He's playing."

Jeanty was a full participant in Wednesday's practice, and Kubiak said he was "excited" about giving his running back more reps in practice.

Jeanty's status for last week's game against the New England Patriots was in question after he missed practice last Friday due to a flare-up of plantar fasciitis, sources told NFL Network's Ian Rapoport. He worked out pregame to determine whether he was good enough to play.

Jeanty, who has not been 100% healthy since sustaining an ankle sprain in late August, had his worst rushing performance of the season in the 45-17 road loss, totaling 27 yards on 10 carries.

In the last four games, Jeanty has averaged 47.3 yards per game.

Despite Jeanty's struggles, he is hoping for a breakout performance at some point.

title: Bears QB Williams unsure if he's playing, has to still go through protocols - ESPN
authors: Courtney Cronin, Bill Barnwell, Jeremy Fowler, Dan Graziano, Matt Bowen, ESPN Fantasy, Nate Taylor, Jordan Raanan, Rich Cimini, Mike Kaye

LAKE FOREST, Ill. -- Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams reached another milestone in his recovery from a hamstring injury Thursday when he logged full participation in practice for the first time since Sept. 18.
Williams has been sidelined for Chicago's last three games while recovering from a hamstring injury sustained late in the fourth quarter of a 9-3 loss to the Minnesota Vikings.

text:
LAKE FOREST, Ill. -- Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams reached another milestone in his recovery from a hamstring injury Thursday when he logged full participation in practice for the first time since Sept. 18.

The Bears quarterback has been listed as a full participant on the team's injury report for two consecutive days, including Wednesday's walk-through, but made clear that his status for Chicago's Week 6 game at Atlanta has not been decided.

"Before you start asking, do not know if I'm playing yet," Williams said. "Have to go through a bunch of medical protocols, obviously have to get out there and practice, do the stress testing that you do when you're trying to come back from injury or serious injury."

Williams has been sidelined for Chicago's last three games while recovering from a hamstring injury sustained late in the fourth quarter of a 9-3 loss to the Minnesota Vikings. Speaking for the first time about the injury and its aftermath, Williams feared the worst after his right leg gave out while he was running toward the end zone with 7:42 to play in the game.

"I felt a pop," Williams said. "That's why I looked back. I looked back just like everybody else does when you feel a pop. Think somebody grabbed you and nobody grabbed me."

Williams said he has had five to six hours of treatment on his hamstring daily and estimates that he was back on the field throwing "probably a week and a half, two weeks" after the injury. While he did not place a percentage on the current strength of his right hamstring, the quarterback said he won't hesitate to run if needed in a game.

"I can move, I can run," Williams said. "I hit a top speed the other day, one of my high speeds I've ever hit and so I can move, I can run, I've got strength. ... Just going through the stress test because obviously fibers and things like that in your hamstrings and muscles have to connect back together to be able to go out there and play a 60-minute game."

Near the end of a near five-minute opening statement, Williams voiced disdain for the way his injury was reported. He claimed that "every single" report was inaccurate and clarified that he suffered a "pretty serious" hamstring tear.

"There's nothing that has come out that has been right about what it is and what it has been," Williams said.

ESPN's Adam Schefter and NFL Network's Ian Rapoport reported that Williams suffered a Grade 2 hamstring strain, which carried a three to four week timeline for recovery. Coach Ben Johnson chose not to rule Williams out for the Bears-Philadelphia Eagles game in Week 3 upon learning the scope of the injury but said he would not practice that week.

"Here's what I know: This guy's a little bit different than the average human being," Johnson said on Sept. 21. "I said that last night. I'll double down on that. He gets back -- he has in the past, a lot faster than what people can anticipate. I'm not putting a timeline on this. We're going to say week-to-week."

Williams declined to reveal what grade his hamstring injury was given by doctors. When asked to provide more clarity on the severity of the injury, Williams refused "because it's not deserving."

Williams also addressed the criticism he received on social media over how he left the Vikings game after he was transported on a cart from the medical tent to the locker room at Soldier Field with a towel draped over his head. Once removing the towel to give the crowd a thumbs-up, Williams' eyes and face were red from crying.

"I'm always going to show emotion, especially when I can't be out there with the guys when something like that happens," he said. "When I went through the draft process, I went to two places, and the two places was here and popped over to the Vikings for a visit as we all know. And they asked me what's the difference between you and everyone else? It's because I care about the team, about the organization, winning, being out there, my teammates, all of that. I care, and that's the biggest thing. This is what I love to do. This puts a smile on my face. It's everything to me, so not being able to be out there was frustrating. That was more of the, the tears or whatever that was and then, you know, the other half of it was just everybody making jokes and all of that, but that doesn't bother me."

The Bears play two games in a five-day span against the Atlanta Falcons on Oct. 18 and the New England Patriots to open the Week 7 slate next Thursday. Williams' focus is on putting himself in position to play against the Falcons and not weighing how the tight turnaround following Week 6 might affect his health.

"If I'm good to go, I'm good to go," Williams said. "If I'm not and we're just not ready, then we got to wait."

text:
Thanks to Braelon Allen’s career-high 116 rushing yards and a dominant pass-rush effort, the Jets ended their losing streak with a much-needed win over the Browns in Week 5. Star wide receiver Garrett Wilson once again provided the main spark through the air, recording 104 of the Jets’ 182 passing yards.

Despite finally returning to the win column, Gang Green’s passing attack continued to struggle in the sloppy conditions. Some of these struggles can be attributed to the absence of receiver Adonai Mitchell, who has missed the last three games with a finger injury.

The severity of the former 2024 second-round pick’s injury had been unknown, adding more frustrating to his absence.

When asked last week about Mitchell’s injury, head coach Aaron Glenn said he didn’t know whether his finger was sprained or fractured, but that he didn’t have surgery on it. Turns out things can change quickly, because on Wednesday, Glenn told reporters that Mitchell underwent a "small procedure" last week.

“(Adonai) did have a small procedure on his hand,” Glenn said. “But the good thing is, man, that he’s moving his hand really, really well.”

(Adonai) waited like a week, week and a half before he had to see how he actually was going to progress and then we wanted to go ahead and get it knocked out.

Aaron Glenn on Adonai Mitchell

With the former Texas Longhorn not at practice Wednesday and Glenn keeping his status as week-to-week, Mitchell appears unlikely to suit up against AFC East rival the Patriots.

Naturally, that makes his looming absence a major concern in Week 6.

Adonai Mitchell injury remains an obstacle for Jets' offense to overcome

Mitchell quickly established himself as New York’s WR2 during the summer workouts, and the former Texas Longhorn has given the Jets another vertical threat alongside Wilson.

He’s been Smith’s favorite target downfield, receiving four targets on passes of 20-plus yards, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. He hauled in one catch for 40 yards against the Titans in Week 1.

Standing at 6'2" and 205 lbs with a blazing 4.34-second 40-yard dash time, this shouldn’t come as much of a surprise. His physical frame and athleticism, combined with his ability to win 50/50 balls, make him an enticing target.

After the first two games, Mitchell ranked second on the team in receptions (9), targets (15), and receiving yards (123).

Since his injury, the rest of the receiving corps hasn’t provided consistent production. While tight end Kenyon Sadiq exploded for seven catches and 105 yards against the Lions in Week 3, he posted two catches for three yards over the next two games. He's also currently battling through the NFL's concussion protocol, leaving his outlook uncertain.

Granted, the Jets were also without Breece Hall, Tim Patrick and Mason Taylor at various points during this stretch, further complicating their passing attack.

Jets have been unable to fill Mitchell’s void

Still, New York has tried to fill Mitchell’s void on the outside by giving Isaiah Williams a larger role in Weeks 3 and 4 before turning to Patrick in Week 5. While both receivers have their own strengths, neither has been as intimidating downfield as Mitchell.

Williams showcased his big-play ability against the Bears, hauling in a 58-yard touchdown in the team’s 23-12 loss. However, much of his production has come at or near the line of scrimmage. Patrick, like Mitchell, is a big receiver, standing at 6'5" and 210 lbs, though he is more of a run-blocking, red-zone threat receiver.

Mitchell’s value isn’t limited to deep plays downfield. He’s also proven he can add value in the intermediate areas and win matchups with his route-running, logging three catches (four targets) for 47 yards at these levels.

With Mitchell out, the Jets are missing a receiver who can take pressure off Wilson and give their passing game another dimension. Through five games, the five-year veteran from Ohio State leads the team in receptions (31), receiving yards (373), and touchdowns (3).

Williams and Patrick can’t replicate Mitchell's production, as each brings a different skill set to the table. Until New York can consistently find ways to create plays at multiple levels, opposing defenses can afford to focus all their attention on Wilson.

That makes it abundantly clear why Mitchell’s continued absence a significant concern heading into Week 6 and beyond.

title: Patriots get good news on injuries: Will A.J. Brown, Christian Gonzalez be ready to go?

At long last, good news on the injury front had arrived for the Patriots.
Gonzalez suffered a shoulder injury in the team's Week 3 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars and had missed both games and every practice since then.

text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. -- A.J. Brown took a knee at the front of the New England Patriots' stretching line to kick off practice and smiled. On the other end of the line was Christian Gonzalez. On a nearby field was Will Campbell.

At long last, good news on the injury front had arrived for the Patriots.

Brown practiced for the first time since suffering a high ankle sprain in the season opener. Gonzalez, the NFL's highest-paid cornerback, expects to return this week from a shoulder injury. And even Campbell, who suffered a sprained knee in Week 5 against the Las Vegas Raiders, wouldn't rule himself out of Sunday's game against the New York Jets, an encouraging sign that he avoided the worst-case scenario.

While the Patriots' season has seemingly flipped after a 1-2 start thanks to a pair of impressive performances from quarterback Drake Maye, they were dealing with injury after injury. Their win over the Raiders was impressive both because of the way they played and because of who they played without.

Now, it seems they won't be short-handed for long.

The biggest news, of course, is the potential return of Brown. The Patriots traded a first-round pick for the wide receiver in the offseason. But they've only had him on the field for essentially one half after he suffered the ankle injury in Week 1 against the Seattle Seahawks. Now, with Maye playing well, the offense could be back close to full speed if Brown plays.

"Huge boost," was how safety Kevin Byard described it. "He's a WR1. Obviously, the past couple weeks our passing game has been playing really well, so he adds another dynamic to that."

Still, it's not a given that Brown will play Sunday against the Jets. His presence at practice Wednesday merely opened a 21-day window for the Patriots to decide when to activate him to the roster. And the decision could be tricky.

Should they rush him back this week only to face … the Jets? Or should they keep him on the shelf for another week, even though Brown's typical routine might be complicated by a truncated schedule ahead of next Thursday's road game against the Chicago Bears? Or should they keep him out of two more games just to be safe?

"He hasn't been out there for four weeks, so we'll get him back out there practicing and see if he's ready to go in a couple days," coach Mike Vrabel said.

The other good news for the Patriots on Wednesday was the return of their best defensive player. Gonzalez suffered a shoulder injury in the team's Week 3 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars and had missed both games and every practice since then. Until Wednesday.

While New England's schedule gets easier in the coming weeks with matchups against the Jets and Miami Dolphins in two of their next three games, Gonzalez is the most important piece of the team's surging defense.

"I'm good now," Gonzalez said Wednesday. "Ready for Sunday. That's what I'm looking forward to."

Perhaps the most surprising bit of positive news Wednesday came from Campbell. The second-year left tackle suffered an injury to the same knee in which he tore his MCL a year ago. The prognosis initially looked bleak. The expectation was he'd miss a few games.

While he still might, Campbell was wearing pads on the team's practice fields on Wednesday afternoon and said he's "taking it day by day."

"It could always be worse," Campbell said. "Not going to put expectations on anything, just going to trust my body and see how I'm feeling."

Campbell has been arguably the Patriots' best offensive lineman thus far. He has bounced back from last year's postseason struggles in impressive fashion. So his presence on the practice field was welcome.

Still, if Campbell can't play, the team will turn to 2026 first-round pick Caleb Lomu at left tackle. In college last season, Lomu played against the Jets' David Bailey, the No. 2 pick in the draft who notched three sacks last weekend to become the front-runner for Defensive Rookie of the Year.

"He's got good power, good speed, good use of his hands," Lomu said. "He's a smart football player. From watching film so far, he's only improved. So it'll be a really good matchup to go against him again."

The Patriots even got good news regarding TreVeyon Henderson, who, in a surprise, was a limited participant in practice despite an ankle injury suffered against the Raiders. Even if he has to miss a game or two, his presence at practice was a sign that he will not land on injured reserve.

It wasn't all great news for the Patriots on Wednesday, however. Starting cornerback Carlton Davis didn't practice and looks like he could miss another game due to a neck injury.

But in the big picture, in this season where the Patriots have been crushed by injuries, placing 19 players on injured reserve, Wednesday registered as a rare bit of good news.

title: Jets reveal Adonai Mitchell had procedure on finger as return timetable remains uncertain
description:
It appears the Jets will be without wide receiver Adonai Mitchell for another week.
Jets coach Aaron Glenn revealed Wednesday that Mitchell had a “small procedure” on the injured finger on his right hand after previously saying that he had not had one.
Mitchell originally injured his finger in practice Sept. 24.
That could explain why the Jets did not place Mitchell on injured reserve.
Sunday’s game with the Patriots would be the fourth game Mitchell has missed.
text:
It appears the Jets will be without wide receiver Adonai Mitchell for another week.

Jets coach Aaron Glenn revealed Wednesday that Mitchell had a “small procedure” on the injured finger on his right hand after previously saying that he had not had one.

Mitchell was listed as not practicing again on Wednesday and Glenn labeled him “week to week,” which usually translates into “he’s not playing” in Glenn-speak.

“The good thing is, man, he’s moving his fingers around really, really well, and I’m still going to put him on this week-to-week deal,” Glenn said.

Mitchell originally injured his finger in practice Sept. 24. Glenn said the next day that Mitchell had caught his finger in a teammate’s jersey and downplayed the injury, but Mitchell was spotted with a large cast/wrap on the hand the next day.

Glenn said Mitchell did not initially have the procedure done, waiting a bit.

That could explain why the Jets did not place Mitchell on injured reserve.

“Well, I think he waited like a week, week and a half before he had to see how he actually was going to progress and then we wanted to go ahead and get it knocked out,” Glenn said.

Sunday’s game with the Patriots would be the fourth game Mitchell has missed.

If the Jets knew it would be four weeks, they could have placed him on injured reserve and brought him back after that time to give themselves a roster spot.

RB Breece Hall (quad), edge Joseph Ossai (ankle) and OG Dylan Parham (knee) did not practice and probably will miss Sunday’s game.

TE Kenyon Sadiq (concussion) was limited, a good sign for his availability Sunday.

S Dane Belton (knee) was also limited.

LB Kiko Mauigoa (quad) was a full participant in practice.

The Jets opened the practice window on rookie WR Omar Cooper Jr. on Wednesday and now have 21 days to add him to the active roster.

He could be activated for Sunday’s game.

Cooper has been on IR since injuring his ankle in the Week 1 win over the Titans.

“More than anything, of a rookie getting the chance to come back and get these reps that he’s been missing, and I think that’s the number one thing,” Glenn said of getting Cooper back. “Obviously, he’s a really good player, but you never want any rookie to actually miss time because the reps are valuable for these guys.”

Glenn chose to have a walk-through Wednesday instead of practice for the second straight week.

Why?

“I just feel like it’s best for our team right now,” Glenn said.

The Patriots opened the practice window on WR A.J. Brown, who has been out with a high-ankle sprain. It is unclear if he will play Sunday. … Patriots CB Christian Gonzalez, who has missed the past two games with a shoulder injury, told reporters in New England that he is playing Sunday. … Rookie edge David Bailey was named AFC Defensive Player of the Week for his three-sack performance against the Browns. … The Jets signed LB Troy Reeder to the practice squad.

text:
The Philadelphia Eagles will be without their starting quarterback this Sunday against the Carolina Panthers, as the team has ruled out Jalen Hurts due to a superficial blood clot.

On Thursday, the Eagles announced that it was believed that Hurts suffered a calf injury during the Week 4 loss to the Los Angeles Rams. After the team traveled to London for their Week 5 matchup with the Jacksonville Jaguars, Hurts underwent an ultrasound that revealed a blood clot. The Eagles' medical staff and doctors concluded Hurts was safe to suit up and play, but did inform the league office about the situation.

During a follow-up ultrasound on Wednesday of this week, the staff discovered movement in Hurts' blood clot, which led the team to rule him out for Sunday.

Read the Eagles' full statement below:

"On Thursday, October 8th, Jalen visited the training room after practice requesting treatment for his calf. He informed the medical staff he had been cleated during the Rams game on October 4th. This was his first treatment session for the calf injury following the game, after having practiced in full both Wednesday and Thursday. On Friday, Jalen received treatment, practiced in full, and was added to the practice report.

"Out of an abundance of caution, an ultrasound was performed on Saturday following the team's flight to London and walkthrough. The ultrasound revealed a superficial blood clot. Our medical staff and doctors in London reviewed the results and concluded that activity and mobility were important and that Jalen could safely play. Doctors recommended a follow-up ultrasound within 72 hours of the game and the return flight to Philadelphia.

"Jalen played without limitation in the game Sunday, received treatment on Monday and Tuesday, and practiced in full on Wednesday, as reflected in the practice report. Throughout our time in London and this week, we have remained in communication with the league office regarding the matter.

"On Wednesday night, a follow-up ultrasound revealed movement in the small blood clot. Jalen will be out for Sunday's game vs. the Panthers as we determine the appropriate course of treatment. His health and safety are our highest priority."

This is something that will have to be monitored closely, and it could force Hurts to miss more than one game. Just hours before the Eagles discovered movement in the blood clot, Hurts addressed the "calf injury" that led him to be listed on the injury report last Friday and on Wednesday.

"It was a very unique experience, to say the least," Hurts said. "I don't want to get into the details of kind of leading up to the game and whatnot, but got nicked up in the Rams game."

The Eagles did not go into detail about the clot, but this could be classified as "superficial thrombophlebitis," per Harvard Health Publishing. This is different than "deep vein thrombosis," which is a much more serious condition that requires anti-clotting drugs. We've seen several cases of deep vein thrombosis in the NBA, including with Spurs superstar Victor Wembanyama, who missed the final 30 games of the 2024-25 season after doctors discovered deep vein thrombosis in his right shoulder. As for superficial thrombophlebitis, Harvard Health Publishing says it can improve over the course of one week to several weeks. Each case is different.

With Hurts out, Tanner McKee is expected to start under center for the Eagles. He's 1-1 in his two career starts over the last two years and has played in a total of six NFL games. In the 2024 regular-season finale, the former sixth-round pick out of Stanford impressed in a 20-13 win over the Giants. McKee completed 27 of 41 passes for 269 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions.

Philly also has rookie Cole Payton on the roster. He was selected in the fifth round of this year's draft out of North Dakota State.

While the Eagles just released Andy Dalton last week, NFL Media reports that the veteran is an option to return. He's reportedly been in contact with a few teams, but he's familiar with Nick Sirianni's offense if the Eagles decide to go that route.

Through five games, Hurts has completed 57.8% of his passes for 933 yards, eight touchdowns and three interceptions in a 2-3 start. Sunday's loss to the Jaguars in London snapped a franchise-record streak of 76 games where the Eagles were .500 or better, per CBS Sports Research.

The Eagles said Hurts "played without limitation" against the Jaguars before receiving treatment Monday and Tuesday then practicing in full Wednesday.

"On Wednesday night, a follow-up ultrasound revealed movement in the small blood clot. Jalen will be out for Sunday's game vs. the Panthers as we determine the appropriate course of treatment. His health and safety are our highest priority," the Eagles said.

The Eagles have remained in communication with the NFL office throughout the process, the team said.

Asked about the injury Wednesday, Hurts indicated he got "nicked" against the Rams while hinting that the lead-up to the Jaguars game was not ordinary.

"It was a very unique experience, to say the least. I don't want to get into the details of kind of leading up to the game and whatnot, but got nicked up in the Rams game," he said.

Hurts did not take the field until right before the opening kickoff against Jacksonville and rode the stationary bike between series. He indicated both actions were related to the calf. He completed 21 of 40 passes for 220 yards and one touchdown in the 19-17 loss to the Jaguars.

Tanner McKee is expected to start in place of Hurts against the Panthers.

The 28-year-old Hurts has 933 passing yards, eight touchdowns and three interceptions this season. He has led the Eagles to two Super Bowl appearances and earned MVP honors after they beat the Kansas City Chiefs to win the championship in the 2024 season.

Hurts is in the midst of a five-year, $255 million extension, including $179.3 million guaranteed, with the Eagles that takes him through the 2028 season.

The Eagles stunned fans when they drafted Hurts out of Oklahoma in the second round in 2020. They seemingly had Carson Wentz entrenched at QB and had more pressing needs. title: First Call: Baker Mayfield health update before Steelers visit Tampa - TribLIVE.com
description:

The NFL addresses concerns about the Steelers-Saints game in Paris next week.
Aaron Rodgers addresses concerns about the Steelers’ wide receiver room this week.

text:
Thursday’s “First Call” checks on Baker Mayfield’s health in advance of the Pittsburgh Steelers’ game in Tampa on Sunday. Some Pitt, Penn State and Duquesne alumni are also on the Buccaneers’ injured list.

The NFL addresses concerns about the Steelers-Saints game in Paris next week. Aaron Rodgers addresses concerns about the Steelers’ wide receiver room this week.

We also get an update on Lamar Jackson’s recovery ahead of the Cleveland-Baltimore showdown in the AFC North.

Working back

Both the Steelers (3-2) and Buccaneers (1-4) had lengthy injury reports to start the week. Several players on both teams didn’t practice at all, with two more workdays to go.

On the Steelers’ side, Keeanu Benton, Jalen Ramsey, Ben Skowronek and Roman Wilson all missed practice entirely with various injuries. Cameron Heyward had a rest day. Skowronek and Wilson are expected to miss the game, based on Mike McCarthy’s statements Monday.

As for Tampa Bay, plenty of familiar names didn’t practice. They include quarterback Baker Mayfield, cornerback Ayden Garnes (Duquesne/WVU), running back Sean Tucker and defensive back Antoine Winfield Jr. Former Penn State receiver Chris Godwin also sat out for a rest day. Ex-Pitt linebacker SirVocea Dennis was limited with ankle and foot injuries.

Mayfield was supposed to be out for three to six weeks with his thumb injury. Last week, he was reportedly hoping to push it to come back for the Pittsburgh game. If he can’t go, Jalon Daniels will start at quarterback.

“Nothing has changed,” coach Todd Bowles said following practice. “He’s getting better. We’ll see how much he throws and how he looks.”

According to the Tampa Bay Times, Bowles said of Mayfield: “If he’s not 100%, he doesn’t need to play.”

No help on the way

Based on how Aaron Rodgers spoke Wednesday, don’t expect the Steelers to add any wide receiver help anytime soon.

That’s despite injuries to Skowronek, Wilson and Michael Pittman Jr.

“It seems like at this point it’s just in-house options. We’ve got a talented (practice) squad group of guys and guys who played football at the highest level and made plays. Excited about getting those guys in,” Rodgers said. “(Brandon) Smith, Brandon Johnson, maybe Isaiah (Hodgins). We’ll get some guys who haven’t seen a lot of time out there and expect them to play well.”

The quarterback also suggested that the tight ends could increase their roles, including Robert Tonyan, who has been used sparingly since being acquired this offseason. He has one catch for 2 yards on one target this season.

“Obviously, (Tonyan) has played a lot of football and played at a high level, so I’m sure he’ll get some more opportunities,” Rodgers added.

Pat Freiermuth had two touchdowns last week. He and Darnell Washington combined for seven catches and 56 yards against the Colts.

More sports

• Steelers excelling in yards after catch because of tackle-breaking, accurate passing

• Pitt tight end Carson Kent embracing expanded role in offense

• Mark Madden: Mike McCarthy can be trusted to make right decisions for Steelers

Familiar foe

Elsewhere in the AFC North, the Cincinnati Bengals are idle this weekend, and the Baltimore Ravens and Cleveland Browns play each other.

That means the Ravens will be facing former offensive coordinator Todd Monken. He’s now coaching the Browns.

When asked if Monken is preparing for Lamar Jackson at quarterback, Monken said, “I think you prepare for the Ravens.”

Jackson is dealing with an ankle injury and missed last week’s win in Atlanta. Jeff Zrebiec of The Athletic quoted Baltimore coach Jesse Minter as saying that Jackson is day-to-day and “when he’s ready, he’ll be out at practice.”

Still on

The Steelers’ game against New Orleans next week is still scheduled to take place in Paris. That’s despite a wave of protests in France.

The league issued a statement to ESPN’s Brooke Pryor that it is still “excited” to have the game overseas.

According to The New York Times, the protests are by students acting out “against poor school conditions and teacher shortages.”

If it is determined that the contest can’t be played in Paris, New Orleans is the designated home team, so the game may well shift to the Caesars Superdome.

text:
TEMPE, Ariz. -- Arizona Cardinals rookie running back Jeremiyah Love did not practice Wednesday to rest his ailing left ankle and his status for Sunday's game against the Rams isn't clear as of yet, coach Mike LaFleur said.

The plan, LaFleur said, is to take Love's ankle "one day at a time," but the Cardinals understand for it to fully heal, the third-overall pick needs to stay off it.

"We all are in agreeance as much as he wants to battle through, we're all in agreeance right now, it's just, hey just give it a little bit of rest and see as the week goes on what that'll entail for Sunday."

Love's style of play, however, makes it difficult for him to prevent the injury from lingering, LaFleur intimated.

"I'm going to try to be as candid as possible with also knowing that everyone's listening to this, too," LaFleur said, "but he's a tough dude. "

But you guys see the way he plays and how aggressive he is with his cuts. And, I mean, imagine being a back in the NFL trying to put the foot down and cut the way that you're capable of?"

Asked whether he was concerned about Love's injury lingering, LaFleur swiftly pointed out which body part was injured.

"They're ankles. It's an ankle," LaFleur said. "So, you don't know. I'm not a doctor and each body's a little bit different. The way he came back from the one in the preseason was unbelievable. I mean, he doesn't even feel it. But this one is the one that happened when the regular season started and it's just lingered."

Love has rushed for 245 yards and one touchdown on 67 carries this season for an average of 3.7 yards per carry. He's also contributed 36 receiving yards and a touchdown on 11 catches. His best game to date came in Week 3 at San Francisco, when he ran for 89 yards.

The Notre Dame star rushed for just 22 yards in Sunday's loss to the Detroit Lions on 12 carries.

LaFleur said, in some ways, Love's explosiveness has been affected by the ankle injury in recent weeks.

"You'd have to ask him that," LaFleur said. "I know how explosive he is. I know how explosive he wants to be. So, I mean, I think that's a fair assessment in some aspects. Again, I don't think it's an overall hindrance, but again, the rest for him is going to be vital."

text:
The NFL’s Week 6 injury picture is starting to take shape, with many teams hoping to welcome back their injured players while others prepare for another week without their stars. Lamar Jackson‘s potential return is encouraging news for the Baltimore Ravens, but there is still uncertainty regarding others.

Baltimore Ravens

According to ESPN’s Adam Schefter, “Ravens QB Lamar Jackson has a realistic chance to return for Sunday’s game at Cleveland, per league source.”

ADVERTISEMENT

ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported that Jackson can return against the Cleveland Browns on Sunday. Ravens HC Jesse Minter also offered a positive update, saying Jackson was definitely doing better.

However, his participation in practice is an important factor before the team makes a final decision. Jackson’s return would provide a boost to the Ravens’ offense. Before his absence, the QB had completed 70.8% of his passes for 967 yards, six TDs, and one INT.

ADVERTISEMENT

Jackson suffered an ankle injury in Week 4. In the meantime, Tyler Huntley led the Ravens to a Week 5 victory over Atlanta, but Jackson’s dual-threat ability is a major part of their offensive plans.

ADVERTISEMENT

Chicago Bears

The Chicago Bears also have reason for optimism regarding their starting quarterback. Caleb Williams was sidelined with a Grade 2 hamstring strain suffered in Week 2, but reports show that he is targeting his return in Week 6 against the Atlanta Falcons.

text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. -- When Adonai Mitchell injured a finger in practice before Week 3, the New York Jets decided not to put the wide receiver on injured reserve, thinking he'd be back within four weeks.

As it turned out, Mitchell underwent surgery about a week later, coach Aaron Glenn revealed Wednesday, and now is expected to miss his fourth consecutive game.

Mitchell is still considered week-to-week, according to Glenn. It means Tim Patrick, who returned last week from a four-week stint on IR, likely will start alongside Garrett Wilson when the Jets (2-3) face the New England Patriots (3-2) on Sunday at Gillette Stadium.

Rookie Omar Cooper Jr., who has missed four games with a high ankle sprain, also could be a factor as he was designated to return from IR.

Mitchell's injury has been a mystery. Glenn has been evasive, claiming last week that he didn't know if the finger was fractured or sprained and saying there was no surgery. On Wednesday, Glenn opened his news conference by saying he wanted to provide "some clarity" on the injury.

"So he did have a small procedure on his hand," Glenn said. "But the good thing is, man, he's moving his fingers around really, really well."

Glenn said Mitchell waited about a week to 10 days before opting for surgery because he wanted "to see how he progressed and then wanted to go ahead and get it knocked out."

Mitchell has remained on the 53-man roster. The Jets could've put him on IR when the injury occurred, which would've created a roster spot for another player. He had nine receptions for 122 yards in the first two games. Since then, the Jets' receivers not named Wilson have produced only seven receptions and one touchdown.

The Jets are hopeful that Cooper, one of the team's three first-round draft picks this spring, can contribute immediately. He lasted only five snaps in the opener before injuring his ankle. One of those plays was a dazzling catch-and-run that covered 30 yards.

"Obviously, he's a really good player, but you never want any rookie to actually miss time because the reps are valuable for these guys," Glenn said of Cooper.

title: Update on NFL Concussion Litigation - Jinks Crow
description:

This syndrome occurs when the brain swells rapidly after a person suffers a second concussion before symptoms from an earlier concussion have subsided.
The settlement provides that the Defendants will pay $1,200,000.00 to The Derek Sheely Foundation.

text:
Now that football season is here, we should be mindful that the highest priority of the game should be the safety and well-being of the athletes. Unfortunately, this has not always been the case.

On August 28, 2011, Derek Sheely died as a result of second-impact syndrome. This syndrome occurs when the brain swells rapidly after a person suffers a second concussion before symptoms from an earlier concussion have subsided. On August 22, 2013, the family of Derek Sheely filed a wrongful death lawsuit against the NCAA, Kranos, George L. Heider, Inc., two Frostburg State University coaches, and a Frostburg State athletic trainer, asserting that Derek’s death was a preventable tragedy.

Last month, the Parties announced that a settlement was reached. The settlement provides that the Defendants will pay $1,200,000.00 to The Derek Sheely Foundation. In addition to this payment, the Parties agreed to the following terms that are aimed at increasing awareness and research about concussions.

The NCAA and FSU, in conjunction with The Derek Sheely Foundation, agreed to sponsor and fund a symposium in honor of Derek Sheely. It will focus on the reduction of catastrophic risk to student-athletes and will be presented to coaches, trainers, sports medicine personnel, student-athletes, youth, and parents.

FSU will establish an annual Derek Sheely Foundation fundraiser on campus.

FSU will provide sufficient funding to enable The Derek Thomson Sheely Leadership Award to be increased to a full-tuition scholarship for a minimum of 10 years, and potentially longer, to begin on or before the 2017-2018 academic year.

The NCAA and FSU, in conjunction with The Derek Sheely Foundation, will make a research award for a project dealing with catastrophic risk.

FSU will retire Derek Sheely’s number and display it in a location on campus.

The NCAA will continue to discuss with its member institutions policies regarding concussion guideline enforcement, concussion, and second-impact syndrome training for coaches and trainers, and elimination of certain drills.

The NCAA will produce a new video addressing risks of head injuries, including second-impact syndrome, in sports that will be available to member institutions on or before June 1, 2017.

Paul Anderson, the attorney for the Sheely Foundation, stated: “This is a tremendous result that will guarantee that The Derek Sheely Foundation will be able to continue its mission of protecting the health and safety of athletes, while also ensuring that Derek’s legacy lives on through the Foundation. This unprecedented litigation and subsequent settlement have solidified that second-impact syndrome is not an inherent risk of sport and that those who are responsible for the safety of athletes must take affirmative action to prevent a tragedy like Derek’s from ever happening again.”

Hopefully, this senseless tragedy will not be in vain. Because of the work of the Sheely Foundation and others to educate and train coaches and their staff, the risks associated with football and other sports can be minimized. This landmark settlement will no doubt go a long way in that regard.

title: Jalen Hurts won't say much about "very unique" calf injury that was disclosed last Friday
description:
Quarterback Jalen Hurts was listed as fully participating in Friday’s practice before the game against the Jaguars with a calf injury.
He had no injury designation for Sunday’s game in London, and he was never downgraded to questionable or doubtful.
What would be “very unique” about a calf injury that didn’t impact his practice reps?
Hurts was listed as a full participant in Wednesday’s practice, due to the calf injury.
And the NFL doesn’t require much more than the bare-bones contents of the injury report.
text:
Last week’s injury report for the Eagles included a curious designation on Friday. And Wednesday’s comments from the player at the center of the issue served only to make it more curious.

Quarterback Jalen Hurts was listed as fully participating in Friday’s practice before the game against the Jaguars with a calf injury. He had no injury designation for Sunday’s game in London, and he was never downgraded to questionable or doubtful.

When the question came up during his midweek press conference, here’s what Hurts said: “It was a very unique experience, to say the least. I don’t want to get into the details of kind of leading up to the game and whatnot, but got nicked up in the Rams game.”

There’s a lot there, in not that many words. What would be “very unique” about a calf injury that didn’t impact his practice reps? And why would it be a big secret?

The complicating factor is that the Eagles flew to London on Friday. Did he require medical care in London? Would it be something that the team doctors were able to provide? Did he have to visit a local hospital for it?

He said he was “nicked up” during the Rams game, but he wasn’t on the injury report for Wednesday or Thursday. Was is it that could have happened on Sunday that would have resulted in symptoms on Friday. (A condition like compartment syndrome typically surfaces much more quickly.)

Regardless, plenty of questions flow from what seems to be very innocuous and basic on the surface. Hurts’s words deepen the mystery.

He remains on the Week 6 injury report, in advance of Sunday’s game against the Panthers. Hurts was listed as a full participant in Wednesday’s practice, due to the calf injury.

Whatever the explanation is, there’s clearly more to the story than what the team has disclosed. And the NFL doesn’t require much more than the bare-bones contents of the injury report.

text:
Wednesday in the NFL brought updates on two quarterbacks working their way back from injury.

The Baltimore Ravens and Chicago Bears provided updates on their situations ahead of the weekend. Lamar Jackson is inching closer to a return for the Ravens, while Caleb Williams took a real step forward in Chicago.

Jackson was absent again from the portion of Ravens practice open to reporters, but there's a "realistic chance" he plays Sunday against the Cleveland Browns. Meanwhile, Williams was a full participant in the Bears’ Wednesday walkthrough, the clearest sign yet that he could be back under center against the Atlanta Falcons.

Here’s the latest from around the NFL on Wednesday.

Bears quarterback Caleb Williams took a real step toward returning for Sunday’s game against the Falcons, serving as a full participant in Chicago’s Wednesday walkthrough after missing the past three weeks with a hamstring injury.

It’s a positive sign that Williams could be back on the field soon, but head coach Ben Johnson didn't rush to say his return would come against Atlanta when asked who would start under center this week.

"It’s still fluid," Johnson told reporters, "but I feel good about the plan that we have in place at this point."

Williams showed progress last week, logging a limited practice and working through pregame warm-ups as he inches closer to a return.

The 2022 Heisman Trophy winner was initially expected to miss three to four games after injuring his hamstring in Week 2, and the Bears went 2-1 without him, with backups Case Keenum and Tyson Bagent each starting and picking up a win, though Bagent struggled in last week’s 31-7 loss to the Packers.

Johnson also acknowledged the tight turnaround before Chicago’s Thursday night game against the Falcons could factor into how the team handles the quarterback's workload regardless of who starts.

"I don't know that any of them are exactly 100% at this point of the season, so that's something that we certainly look at," Johnson said.

Running back Saquon Barkley and Wide Receiver DeVonta Smith both sat out again Wednesday as the Eagles opened their practice week ahead of Sunday’s game against the Panthers, both still nursing hamstring injuries.

Barkley missed last week’s game in London after playing just four snaps against the Rams the week prior, and Smith has now missed the last two games.

Philadelphia’s offense has cratered without its two biggest weapons as the Eagles have managed just 404 total yards over those two losses.

Earlier in the week, head coach Nick Sirianni told reporters he was "hopeful" one or both could return this week.

The need is especially urgent at running back, where backup Tank Bigsby is on injured reserve and third-stringer Will Shipley is now expected to miss multiple weeks with a foot injury suffered against the Jaguars.

That left Philadelphia finishing that game with two practice-squad call-ups, Dameon Pierce and Carson Steele, and just 22 rushing yards on 18 carries — the team’s lowest rushing output in a game since 2015.

Barkley and Smith are far from the only Eagles players dealing with injuries as six players sat out Wednesday’s practice in total, while 11 other players were limited participants. Seven more Eagles players were listed as full participants on Wednesday's injury report, including quarterback Jalen Hurts (calf).

Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson was missing again from the open portion of Ravens' practice Wednesday as he continues working back from the ankle injury that’s already cost him one game.

Ravens Head Coach Jesse Minter said Wednesday that Jackson was "definitely day-to-day" adding, "To Lamar’s credit, he’s working his butt off and he's doing everything he can to be out here." ESPN reported Wednesday that Jackson has a "realistic chance" to play Sunday.

Jackson went down two weeks ago in a win over the Titans, sacked on the final play of the first half with a sprained left ankle. He completed 15 of 20 passes for 222 yards and two touchdowns before having to leave the game.

Tyler Huntley has stepped in his place after filling in for Jackson nearly half of last season, throwing for 201 yards and two scores and rushing for the winning touchdown in overtime of last week’s win over the Falcons.

At 4-1, Baltimore has some margin to be careful with Jackson’s return, especially after last season’s hamstring injury lingered well past his initial comeback.

Atlanta Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr. isn't expected to be sidelined long after exiting late against the Baltimore Ravens with a rib injury.

Since suffering a high-ankle sprain in Week 1, wide receiver A.J. Brown has been on injured reserve, but his return could take place as early as Sunday. Head coach Mike Vrabel announced Wednesday that Brown has been designated to return to practice.

Brown returned to practice on Wednesday in a limited capacity as he works his way back to full strength.

The Patriots acquired Brown from the Philadelphia Eagles this offseason for a 2028 first-round pick. The offense has had plenty of ups and downs since his injury, but both Romeo Doubs and Efton Chism III have seen steady improvements in production since.

Getting Brown back into an improving offense will be huge for Drake Maye as the Patriots push to stay competitive in the AFC playoff picture.

Head coach Kevin Stefanski told reporters on Wednesday that Michael Penix Jr. is expected to start against the Chicago Bears, barring any setbacks. Since entering the league, he has struggled to stay healthy, so avoiding missed time is a positive sign for both Penix and the Falcons.

Following Penix’s exit against the Ravens, backup quarterback Tua Tagovailoa came in and threw a game-ending interception in overtime. Before his injury, Penix was having a strong outing, throwing for 240 yards and a touchdown.

Through his first three starts this season, Penix is off to the best stretch of his career, especially impressive considering he's returning from a season-ending knee injury. He's completed 67.5% of his passes for 719 yards, three touchdowns, and just one interception.

Keeping Penix on the field is massive for a Falcons team competing in a wide-open NFC South. With both Atlanta and Chicago sitting at 3-2, Caleb Williams and Penix are set to face off in a must-win game for both sides.
